title: How long does the trip take at a faster speed?
description: A father rides from Lucknow to Kanpur in two hours at fifty kilometres an hour. The video finds the time at seventy five kilometres an hour from the distance, and shows why the Rule of Three fails here. Keeko doubts this and uses the Rule of Three to get three hours.
teaching_notes: One idea: speed and time are not in proportion, because a higher speed means less time, so the distance is used instead. Watch for students who write fifty to two as seventy five to a missing time and get three hours.

source: {{NAME_6}}'s father rides from Lucknow to Kanpur in 2 hours at 50 km/h. How long does the trip take at 75 km/h?
video_script.why: The child sees that a higher speed gives a shorter time, so speed and time are not in proportion and the distance must be used.
video_script.substitution: Find the distance from the first ride, then divide it by the new speed.
video_script.anchor: a father on a motorcycle riding the road from Lucknow to Kanpur, from the book
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko writes fifty to two as seventy five to a missing time and finds two times seventy five divided by fifty, which gives three hours, more time at a higher speed.
video_script.payoff_line: The trip takes one hour twenty minutes

final_answer.value: 1 hour 20 minutes; speed and time are not proportional, so the Rule of Three does not apply
final_answer.spoken: one hour twenty minutes, because speed and time are not in proportion and the Rule of Three does not apply

names.{{NAME_6}}: the child whose father's trip shows a change that is not proportional

never_show: 3 hours marked as the time at 75 km/h
maths_rules: distance: 50 × 2 = 100 km, the same for both rides
4/3 = 1 + 1/3; 1/3 of 60 minutes = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes, so 1 hour 20 minutes
Keeko's slip: 2 × 75 ÷ 50 = 3 hours, which is more than 2 hours at a higher speed
video_script.design: One idea: a higher speed means less time, so speed and time are not in proportion and the fixed distance gives the answer. The road stays on the stage and the working sits on the board.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a road from Lucknow to Kanpur with a motorcycle, a speed tag 50 km/h and a clock tag 2 hours; then a faster tag 75 km/h with a question mark clock

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.ride: the motorcycle rides the road from Lucknow to Kanpur with the tags 50 km/h and 2 hours
marks.fast: a faster tag 75 km/h appears and a question mark clock appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about {{NAME_6}}'s father.
<bookmark mark='ride'/>{{NAME_6}}'s father rides from Lucknow to Kanpur in two hours at fifty kilometres an hour.
<bookmark mark='fast'/>How long will the same trip take if the speed is seventy five kilometres an hour?

beats.on_screen: the motorcycle holds still and the question mark clock glows

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: two bars grow together to show a proportion; then a speed bar goes up while a time bar goes down; the words Rule of Three appear under the first pair

marks.double: two bars double together to show a proportion
marks.name: the words Rule of Three appear under the pair of bars
marks.opposite: the speed bar goes up while the time bar goes down

narration: <bookmark mark='double'/>In a proportion, when one quantity becomes double, the other quantity also becomes double.
<bookmark mark='name'/>We call the method of finding a missing term from a proportion the Rule of Three.
<bookmark mark='opposite'/>But riding faster takes less time, so we must test if a proportion even exists.

beats.on_screen: Given: 50 km/h takes 2 hours; the new speed is 75 km/h

marks.given: the speed, the time and the new speed are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the trip takes two hours at fifty kilometres an hour. The new speed is seventy five kilometres an hour.

beats.on_screen: To find: the time at the new speed

marks.find: the thing to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the time the trip takes at the new speed.
<bookmark mark='dist'/>Step one, the road is the same for both rides. Fifty times two gives a distance of one hundred kilometres.
<bookmark mark='time'/>Step two, the time is the distance divided by the speed. One hundred divided by seventy five is four thirds of an hour.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Step three, four thirds is one and one third.
<bookmark mark='third'/>One third of an hour is sixty divided by three, which is twenty minutes.

beats.on_screen: check: 75 × 4/3 = 100; the new time is less than 2 hours

marks.less: the new time is marked as less than the old time

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check. Seventy five times four thirds is one hundred, the same distance as before.
<bookmark mark='less'/>The speed went up and the time went down, so they are not in proportion.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 1 hour 20 minutes; speed and time are not proportional, so the Rule of Three does not apply

marks.ans: the answer is boxed beside the motorcycle at the end of the road

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The trip takes one hour twenty minutes.
Speed and time are not in proportion, so the Rule of Three does not apply.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 50 : 2 :: 75 : t and t = 2 × 75 ÷ 50 = 3; a slow motorcycle and a faster one reach the end together in the bubble; the bubble is struck through and 100 ÷ 75 is written

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble appears with 50 : 2 :: 75 : t and t = 2 × 75 ÷ 50 = 3
marks.fast: a faster motorcycle is shown reaching Kanpur before the slower one
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and 100 ÷ 75 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko uses the Rule of Three and thinks the trip takes three hours.
<bookmark mark='fast'/>But a faster ride cannot take more time than a slower ride.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Speed and time move in opposite ways, so we must work from the distance that stays fixed.
